title: Graph Scaling via Generalized Graphon Theory
one_liner: Train a graph model on a small graph, then use it on a much larger graph by tracking how the edge density changes instead of assuming it stays the same.
lead: Graph neural networks learn patterns from one graph. When you want to apply that trained model to a different-sized graph, the number of connections per node usually changes. This paper shows that a model trained on a small graph can work on a large sparse graph if you account for how the connection pattern scales up—a problem no one had a formula for before.

problem.h2: Why graph models don't transfer across sizes
paras: A graph neural network learns from patterns in a graph by looking at each node and its neighbors. When you train a model on a small graph with, say, 1000 nodes, the average node has a few neighbors. If you take that exact trained model and run it on a much larger graph with 100,000 nodes where each node still has just a few neighbors on average, something breaks. The model was tuned to a specific neighborhood pattern—one where most nodes connect to a small fraction of other nodes.

A beginner might think: the learned rules should just work everywhere. But graphs are strange. As you grow a graph while keeping the connection density the same (same fraction of possible edges), the raw number of neighbors changes, and the statistical properties of the neighborhood shift. The model was trained on one noise pattern and gets a different noise pattern on the new graph. There is no formula that says how to measure or fix this mismatch across arbitrary sparsity (any density, no matter how thin the graph is).

callout.html: The paper derives a mathematical bound that predicts how much a model trained on one graph will fail on a larger graph with different connection density.

panels.title: 1. Start
panels.caption: A small graph: 10 nodes, each with a few neighbors. Model learns local patterns.

panels.title: 2. The transfer problem
panels.caption: Apply to a big graph: 10,000 nodes. Same fraction of edges, but each node now has 100 neighbors instead of 5. Statistics are different.

panels.title: 3. Old theory fails
panels.viz_args: Classical graphon vanishes in sparse graphs. No error bound.
panels.caption: Previous theory assumes graphs get dense. In sparse real networks, the math breaks. No prediction of transfer error.

panels.title: 4. Generalized graphon
panels.caption: Stretch the graph to preserve topology even when sparse. Error separates into size and density effects.

panels.title: 5. Prediction works
panels.viz_args: Error vanishes as graph grows and density drops.
panels.caption: Now you can predict how much the model will drift—and know the rule works for any sparsity.

steps.text: A graph neural network learns connection patterns from a source graph.
Count edges and nodes in both source and target graphs to compute how sparse each one is.
Generalized graphon theory says: if edge density is different, apply a stretching transformation to match topological structure.
The paper's formula decomposes transfer error into two parts: one that shrinks with larger graphs, one from density mismatch.

Run the trained model on the new graph knowing the error bound. As the target graph grows larger, random noise in each node's neighborhood gets averaged out across more independent nodes, so the size-dependent error term shrinks by the square root of the size increase.

paras: The paper introduces a new way to represent graphs mathematically so that transferring a learned model across graphs of different sizes produces a provable error bound. It uses generalized graphon theory (a framework from graph mathematics that studies limits of large graphs) instead of classical graphon limits.
object.object: the mathematical limit representation of a graph

hidden.name: transfer error decomposition
paras: The paper measures one hidden quantity: how far off the model's output becomes when you move from the training graph to a new target graph. This is the transfer error—the gap between what the model predicts on the source graph versus on the target graph.

This error has two components: a size-dependent part (which goes down as the target graph gets bigger) and a density-dependent part (which depends on the difference in how many edges each node has on average). The paper derives explicit formulas for both parts.

heat.caption: Darker means more impact on transfer error. Highlights show core quantities the paper uses.

reads.html: Transfer error is how wrong the model gets when you switch graphs. The paper splits this into one part that improves as you make the target graph bigger—because larger graphs have more nodes to average out random noise—and another part that depends on how much the connection density changed, since graphs with different edge counts per node have fundamentally different patterns.

The explicit error bound is derived from generalized graphon theory and decomposes into size-dependent and density-dependent components that characterize the convergence rate across arbitrary sparsity regimes.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: the three-step logic
paras: Classical graphon theory studies what happens to a graph as it grows infinitely large and dense. It draws a mathematical limit (a graphon function) that describes the edge pattern. The problem: in sparse graphs—where most pairs of nodes are not connected—this limit vanishes to zero and tells you nothing.

The paper's fix is to apply stretching. Think of it this way: instead of asking what happens when a sparse graph grows while staying sparse, ask what happens when you blow up the distance between nodes so that the density appears to stay constant. The graphon does not vanish anymore; it remains a real, usable object. The stretching factor is just a number you compute from how sparse the target graph is.

Once the graphon is non-trivial, you can bound the error. The paper proves: the error you get when transferring a model is bounded by two things: how many new nodes the target graph has (bigger graphs have more noise to average out, so error shrinks) and the ratio of edge densities (graphs with very different connection patterns have more fundamental mismatch). Both effects are made quantitative in closed-form equations.

stages.s: Small source graph (trained model) and large target graph (different density)
Compute density ratio: edges per node source vs target
Apply stretching transformation to preserve graph topology even when sparse
Extract graphon limit (the mathematical essence of edge patterns)
Bound transfer error as sum of size-dependent and density-dependent terms
Error formula valid for any sparsity; predicts model accuracy drop

math.words: Transfer error equals a size component (gets smaller as the target graph grows) plus a density component (depends on how different the edge densities are). Both are made precise by the graphon limit.
math.equation: error_transfer <= c1 * sqrt(log(n_target) / n_target) + c2 * |rho_source - rho_target|
symbols: the prediction error gap when moving from source to target graph
a constant that depends on the spectral properties of the graphon
a constant that depends on how the model responds to density changes
the number of nodes in the target graph
the edge density in the source graph (fraction of possible edges that exist)
the edge density in the target graph

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the source graph has 100 nodes with density 0.1 (10 edges per node on average), and the target has 10,000 nodes with density 0.05 (5 edges per node on average).
Size term: sqrt(log(10000) / 10000) = sqrt(4 / 10000) = 0.02. Multiply by c1 = 0.5 gives 0.01 error contribution.
Density term: |0.1 - 0.05| = 0.05. Multiply by c2 = 0.2 gives 0.01 error contribution.
Total error bound: 0.01 + 0.01 = 0.02 (2% model accuracy drop). As n_target grows to 1 million, the size term shrinks to 0.005, but the density mismatch stays at 0.01.

math.note: The size term shrinks with the square root of graph size (more nodes average out more noise), while the density term is constant and depends only on how much the connection patterns differ.

charts.title: Naive transfer (no correction)
charts.note: Without accounting for density change, the model fails badly on the new graph.

charts.title: This paper (with error bound)
charts.note: By correcting for density differences via generalized graphon theory, the model maintains performance and you know the error in advance.

items.b: Source and target graphs have fundamentally different structure.
items.html: The error bound assumes both graphs are in a similar class (e.g., both social networks or both biological networks). If the source is dense and clustered but the target is tree-like and sparse, the error bound may be loose because the model learned from a very different topology.

If the source graph is very dense (density 0.8) and the target is extremely sparse (density 0.001), the density-dependent error term becomes large. The bound says transfer is still possible but warns you the error will be significant.

items.b: Graph is too small to reach asymptotic regime.
items.html: The formula assumes the size-dependent term dominates for large graphs. On graphs with just 100 nodes, the square-root convergence may not kick in yet, and the bound is less tight.

items.b: Large regular graphs with matching density.
items.html: When source and target have the same edge density and both are large, the error bound shrinks to near-zero, and transfer works nearly perfectly.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple graph neural network (a model that reads node features by summing neighbor features and applying a learned transformation) on a small, synthetic graph with 100 nodes and average degree 5. Train it on a node classification task (predicting a label for each node). Then apply the same trained model to three target graphs: one with 1000 nodes at degree 5 (matching density), one with 1000 nodes at degree 2 (sparser), and one with 1000 nodes at degree 10 (denser). For each, measure the actual error gap between source and target. Plot error versus target graph size for each density ratio. Then, compute the generalized graphon error bound for each case using the paper's formula. The prediction should match the measured error trend and show that error shrinks as target size grows.
demo.closing: The demo must show that the paper's error bound correctly predicts how the model's accuracy falls as you move to denser or sparser graphs (because different densities mean different neighborhood patterns the model never saw), and that the bound gets tighter (model does better) as the target graph grows (because larger graphs average out statistical fluctuations).
